extracted.intended_audience: professional and aspiring photographers/photojournalists and social photo editors who want to be featured on major news-organizations' Instagram accounts (specifically those pitching or producing content for The New York Times' social accounts).
extracted.subtask_short: instagram photo curation for news orgs
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and informal standards for selecting, captioning, and pitching photography for a major news organization's Instagram and archival accounts, plus how social photo editors find and evaluate photographers. Useful for photographers who want to be featured and editors who curate social-photo content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Think about visual presentation across social platforms
rubrics_metrics.description: The Social Photo Editor's job is to think about visual presentation across social media—primarily Facebook, Twitter and Instagram—and curate images accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider how images read on each platform and the newsroom's presence there; curate for platform-specific audiences and formats rather than treating social as an afterthought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Represent the breadth of newsroom coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: The goal is to feature work by the paper's wide network of photographers and represent the breadth of New York Times coverage (food photography, celebrity portraiture, reportage-style work, daily life).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intentionally include diverse beats and styles so followers see the range of the paper's photography; balance newsy reportage with lifestyle and feature imagery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account-specific tone: @nytimes vs @nytarchives
rubrics_metrics.description: @nytimes aims for a reflective tone and focuses on the best of visual news and daily-life moments; @nytarchives is meant to be fun, aiming for surprise and delight with archival images and a fairly informal tone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: @nytarchives should not be framed as teaching history or 'this day in history' content; instead provide interesting background that complements eye-catching archival photos.

rubrics_metrics.name: Captions are as important as the images
rubrics_metrics.description: Captions should tell full (albeit short) New York Times stories that are written to the photograph; they can be conversational, include the subject's voice, or use reporters' wording when appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When possible include the story behind the photo (e.g., how the photographer reached the spot, whether they were in a helicopter or walked for hours); be mindful that some users scroll quickly, but many do read captions—write to reward those readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use subject voice and contextual detail in captions
rubrics_metrics.description: If using a picture of a person, include that person's voice; provide context about how and why the photograph was made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small details (who, where, how) enrich engagement and make captions feel grounded and authoritative—e.g., 'the photographer walked six hours to reach this spot.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Preferred pitching format and required materials
rubrics_metrics.description: Photographers should pitch via email with a brief synopsis and additional information attached, and include more than just a few images so editors can tell if a project is working.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Email is preferred because it’s easy to share with other Times editors. Attach a concise synopsis and multiple images or contact sheets rather than relying on single-image pitches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common pitching mistakes to avoid
rubrics_metrics.description: Frequent errors include overly wordy pitches, not including enough photos, pitching via Facebook Messenger, and using incorrect forms of address (e.g., calling a female editor 'sir').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep pitches concise, include sufficient imagery for evaluation, use professional channels (email), and address editors respectfully and correctly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Where editors look to discover photographers
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors pay attention to bylines and follow many photographers on social media; they use Instagram digging and follow large numbers of accounts to discover work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain clear bylines/credits on published work, be active and consistent on social platforms, and curate personal work but be mindful of employer/organization policies regarding sharing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Credit and attribution practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Photographers should have clear bylines and be credited when their work is featured (the editor notes paying attention to bylines and regramming with photographer attribution).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure published pieces and social posts include correct photographer credits; when pitching, include name and affiliation so editors can attribute properly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection prioritization under high volume
rubrics_metrics.description: A major challenge is the sheer amount of strong photography available; editors must prioritize and select images that best represent coverage and storytelling needs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Photographers should submit only their strongest work with clear story value; editors balance visual interest, narrative potential, and representational variety when choosing what to feature.
